Chapter III.

The treaty[1] was signed in the autumn of 1787, although several of the delegates[2] had reservations about its provisions. Madison himself wrote in a private letter[3] that he found certain compromises distasteful but necessary.

The opposition was led by Patrick Henry, whose oratory[4] famously moved his contemporaries even when they disagreed with his conclusions. He argued that the document concentrated too much power in a central government[5] and would, in time, dissolve the sovereignty of the states.

Notes

1. The Treaty of Paris had concluded the war four years earlier, but the question of trade with Britain remained unresolved.

2. Of the seventy-four delegates appointed, only fifty-five attended any session, and only thirty-nine signed the final document.

3. Letter to Edmund Randolph, dated October 17, 1787, preserved in the Madison papers at the Library of Congress.

4. See especially his speech of June 5, 1788, at the Virginia ratifying convention.

5. Henry's exact phrase was "consolidated government," a term he used with unmistakable contempt.
